content: 1. Therapeutic or dose equivalence is explicitly evaluated and stated using a well-established methodology. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the use of value-based pricing for medicines to support price setting and reimbursement decisions under specific conditions: Value-based pricing should be combined with other pricing policies, such as price negotiation, internal and external reference pricing, and policies promoting the use of quality-assured generic and biosimilar medicines. Adequate resources and skilled personnel must be available to implement value-based pricing effectively. Value-based pricing using health technology assessment (HTA) must include an analysis of budget impact and affordability from the perspectives of both payers and patients. A robust governance structure for value-based pricing using HTA should be in place to ensure transparency in processes, with public dissemination of assessment reports and decisions. The methods and perspectives used to determine value must be explicitly defined. Decisions and evidence should undergo periodic review and reassessment. 3. WHO advises countries to ensure transparency in pricing and methods when establishing mark-ups along the supply and distribution chain, including disclosure of any rebates and discounts. 4. WHO recommends regular reviews of mark-up regulations to protect patients from excessive out-of-pocket expenditures. 5. Pricing equivalence for pharmaceutical products should be determined using the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical Classification System (4th level) based on clinical trial evidence of non-inferiority. 6. WHO suggests improving pricing transparency through mechanisms such as: Sharing net transaction prices of pharmaceutical products with relevant stakeholders, both domestically and internationally. Disclosing prices along the supply and distribution chain. Publicly reporting research and development (R&D) contributions from all sources. Communicating pricing and reimbursement decisions to the public. 7. WHO recommends the use of tendering for pharmaceutical products under the following conditions: Price levels should be considered alongside other criteria, including product quality, characteristics, availability, supply security, reliability, and supply chain charges. Tendering should be complemented by other pricing policies to enhance affordability and availability. 8. WHO advises countries to use price negotiation alongside tendering and other pricing policies. 9. WHO recommends enabling early market entry of generic and biosimilar medicines through legislative and administrative measures. This includes encouraging early submission of regulatory applications, ensuring prompt and effective review, and guaranteeing the safety, efficacy, and quality of these products. 10. WHO suggests countries adopt multiple pricing policies to achieve low prices for generic and biosimilar medicines, informed by production costs. These policies may include internal reference pricing, mark-up regulation, direct price controls, tendering, promoting price transparency, and reducing patient co-payments. 11. To maximize the uptake of generic and biosimilar medicines, WHO recommends implementing and enforcing policies such as: Legislation allowing generic substitution by dispensers and, where applicable, biosimilar substitution. Legislative structures and incentives for prescribers to prescribe by International Nonproprietary Name (INN). Dispensing fees that encourage the use of low-priced generic and biosimilar medicines. Regressive mark-up structures, where lower mark-up rates are applied to higher-priced products, along with appropriate financial and non-financial incentives for dispensers. Educational programs for consumers and professionals on the quality, safety, efficacy, and pricing of generic and biosimilar medicines. 12. WHO recommends the use of pooled procurement of medicines under the following conditions: Pooled procurement should be combined with other pricing policies, such as tendering and negotiation. Procurement processes must be transparent and supported by high standards of governance. Financing for pooled procurement must be sustainable, predictable, and timely, with dedicated resources mobilized for a capitalization fund to stabilize initial regional pooled procurement efforts. 13. WHO advises against using cost-plus pricing as a primary policy for setting pharmaceutical prices due to the current lack of transparency and an agreed framework among stakeholders regarding inputs for price determination. 14. WHO suggests countries consider exempting essential medicines and active pharmaceutical ingredients from taxation. Any tax reductions or exemptions should be accompanied by measures to ensure that the policy results in lower medicine prices for patients and purchasers. 15. The WHO guideline emphasizes the importance of achieving affordable and equitable access to quality-assured pharmaceutical products for consumers and health systems. This aligns with global efforts toward universal health coverage, which includes financial risk protection, access to quality essential health-care services, and access to safe, effective, quality, and affordable essential medicines and vaccines for all. 16. High pharmaceutical prices continue to pose significant challenges globally, impairing the ability of health-care systems to provide population-wide access. In the absence of insurance coverage, patients and their families often face catastrophic financial hardship when in need of medicines. Conversely, excessively low prices may lead to insufficient profit margins for commercial participants, potentially causing medicine shortages, supply interruptions, and negative health outcomes. 17. WHO is mandated to support Member States through policy guidance on pharmaceutical pricing, focusing on promoting competition to improve the availability and affordability of health products consistent with public health policies and needs. 18. The guideline provides evidence-informed recommendations to guide countries in formulating and implementing policies related to price management and access to pharmaceutical products. It replaces the 2015 WHO Guideline on country pharmaceutical pricing policies. 19. The guideline encourages readers to interpret the evidence and consider its recommendations in the context of their respective health systems. It advises considering all policy options that could affect the pricing, affordability, and accessibility of pharmaceutical products, including those beyond the scope of this guideline. 20. The primary audience for this guideline includes policymakers and decision-makers responsible for introducing and revising price-management policies to improve access to pharmaceutical products. It is also intended for managers, operational personnel, donors, development partners, and other stakeholders involved in the pharmaceutical sector. 21. The guideline focuses on two key questions: Which pharmaceutical pricing policies are effective in managing prices, considering their impacts on volume, availability, and affordability? What contextual factors and implementation strategies influence the effects of specific pricing policies? 22. The guideline covers ten pricing policies, including external reference pricing, internal reference pricing, value-based pricing, mark-up regulation, promoting price transparency, tendering and negotiation, promoting the use of quality-assured generic and biosimilar medicines, pooled procurement, cost-plus pricing, and tax exemptions or reductions for pharmaceutical products.
